name: Concentration-Time Graphs
what: This subtopic covers how to sketch and interpret concentration-time graphs for homogeneous equilibrium systems, including how to represent changes in temperature, concentration, pressure, and volume on these graphs.
why: Concentration-time graphs are a direct and frequently assessed representation of equilibrium behaviour in VCE Chemistry. Being able to both sketch and interpret these graphs demonstrates a deep understanding of equilibrium dynamics.

items.title: I can sketch a concentration-time graph to represent an equilibrium system reaching equilibrium from initial conditions
items.what: Starting from initial concentrations of reactants only (products at zero), reactant concentrations decrease and product concentrations increase, both at a decreasing rate, until they reach a constant value at equilibrium. The rate of change gradually slows as equilibrium is approached.
items.why: This base graph shape underpins all more complex graph questions. Students who cannot draw the initial approach to equilibrium correctly will also make errors when adding perturbations to the graph.
items.example: For N2(g) + 2O2(g) = 2NO2(g) starting with only N2 and O2 present, the concentrations of N2 and O2 curve downward and NO2 curves upward, all flattening to constant horizontal lines once equilibrium is reached.

items.title: I can sketch a concentration-time graph showing the effect of adding a reactant to a system at equilibrium
items.what: When a reactant is added, its concentration jumps discontinuously upward. The system then re-establishes equilibrium: the added reactant's concentration decreases, other reactant concentrations decrease slightly, and product concentrations increase, all reaching new constant values.
items.why: This graph type is a standard VCE question. Students need to correctly show the discontinuous jump and then the gradual re-equilibration, and the final equilibrium concentrations must be consistent with Le Chatelier's prediction.
items.example: In the N2 + 2O2 = 2NO2 system at equilibrium, if N2 is added, the graph shows a sharp upward step for N2, then N2 gradually decreases (but settles higher than before), O2 decreases slightly, and NO2 increases to a higher constant level.

items.title: I can sketch a concentration-time graph showing the effect of a temperature change on an equilibrium system
items.what: A temperature change causes all concentrations to shift continuously (no discontinuous jump) until a new equilibrium is reached at different concentration values. The new K value is different from the original, so the final concentration ratio changes.
items.why: Unlike concentration changes, temperature changes affect K itself. This means the final concentration ratios are different, which should be visible on the graph. Students must distinguish this from other perturbations where K does not change.
items.example: For 2NO2(g) = N2O4(g) (exothermic), increasing temperature causes [NO2] to increase and [N2O4] to decrease until a new equilibrium is established at a lower K value. Both curves change simultaneously with no discontinuous jump.

items.title: I can interpret a concentration-time graph to identify what change was made to an equilibrium system
items.what: By examining the shape of the curves, the direction of concentration changes, whether there is a discontinuous jump, and whether the final concentration ratios have changed, it is possible to identify what perturbation was applied to the system.
items.why: Interpreting graphs is assessed in both the school-assessed coursework and the end-of-year examination. It requires integrating understanding of all Le Chatelier scenarios rather than applying them in isolation.
items.example: If a graph shows all concentrations changing continuously (no jump) with some increasing and some decreasing, and the final ratio of products to reactants is different from before the change, this is consistent with a temperature change. A sudden step in one species' concentration points to an addition of that species.
